title: How Muslims Ruled Spain for 781 Years (and Lost It All)
backups: Al-Andalus: The Muslim Kingdom That Lit Up Europe
Why the Last Muslim King of Spain Wept
desc:
On 2 January 1492 the last Muslim king in Western Europe handed the keys of the Alhambra to Ferdinand and Isabella, and that ended a story 781 years long. In 711 a small army crossed from Africa under Tariq ibn Ziyad, landed below a rock that still carries his name, Gibraltar, and took almost the whole peninsula in seven years.

This is Part 1 of our Spain series. A runaway prince swims a river to escape a massacre and founds the emirate of Cordoba. Cordoba grows into one of the biggest cities on Earth, with paved, lamp-lit streets, a huge library, new crops and a man who tried to fly. Then the caliphate breaks into rival kingdoms, the Christian north pushes south, and Granada holds out for 250 years before 1492 changes everything: the surrender, the broken promises, the expulsions, and the Arabic words still spoken in Spain today.

sources: Hugh Kennedy, Muslim Spain and Portugal (1996); Maria Rosa Menocal, The Ornament of the World (2002); Richard Fletcher, Moorish Spain (1992); L. P. Harvey, Islamic Spain 1250-1500 (1990) and Muslims in Spain 1500-1614 (2005); Joseph O'Callaghan, Reconquest and Crusade in Medieval Spain (2003); Encyclopaedia Britannica entries on Al-Andalus, the Umayyad emirate of Cordoba and the Treaty of Granada.
note: Population figures for medieval Cordoba, the library's size and the stories of Tariq burning his boats, Ibn Firnas's flight and Boabdil's last sigh come from chroniclers and later legend and are presented as such.
